title: NTA UGC NET English Full Mock Test #20
subtitle: 100 Questions · 200 Marks · Post-2018 NTA Pattern · Zero Answer Bias (25 A/B/C/D) · Reading Comprehension (Q91-100)

items.title: Mock #20 · Q1
items.stem:
Match the character with the work :
(a)
Jim Dixon
(i)
Room at the Top
(b)
Jimmy Porter
(ii)
Hurry on Down
(c)
Joe Lampton
(iii)
Look Back In Anger
(d)
Charles Lumley
(iv)
Lucky Jim
Code :
(a)
(b)
(c)
(d)
items.explanation: These 1950s 'Angry Young Men' protagonists match their works as follows: (a) Jim Dixon in Kingsley Amis's Lucky Jim (iv); (b) Jimmy Porter in John Osborne's Look Back in Anger (iii); (c) Joe Lampton in John Braine's Room at the Top (i); and (d) Charles Lumley in John Wain's Hurry On Down (ii).

items.title: Mock #20 · Q2
items.stem:
Which 19th century novelist expressed a wish to "exterminate the race" of Indians following
the 1857 Mutiny in India ?
items.explanation: In a notorious letter to philanthropist Angela Burdett-Coutts on 4 October 1857 following the Indian Rebellion of 1857, Charles Dickens wrote that if he were Commander-in-Chief in India, he would do his utmost 'to exterminate the Race upon whom the stain of the late cruelties rested'.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q3
items.stem:
Jonathan Swift arrived in London in 1710 and confronted a rapidly changing world in the new Tory ministry. His reactions to this world are vividly recorded in his Journal to Stella, a series of letters addressed to
(i) Hester Vanhomrigh
(ii) Esther Johnson
(iii) Rebecca Dingley
(iv) Lady Mary Montagu
The right combination according to the code is :
items.explanation: The Journal to Stella was addressed to Esther Johnson (Stella) and her companion Rebecca Dingley.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q4
items.stem: Which of the following statements are not true about Margaret Laurence's Novel, The Stone Angel ? Code : I. The novel is set in a fictional small town in Manitoba called Manawaka. II. The novel was written when she was away from Canada. III. The novel is narrated retrospectively by Hagar Shipley. IV. The novel is least known of her works. The correct combination according to the code is
items.explanation: Margaret Laurence's The Stone Angel (1964) is her most famous masterpiece rather than her least known work (making IV false). It is the first of her 'Manawaka' novels set in a fictional Manitoba town (I) and is narrated retrospectively by the ninety-year-old protagonist Hagar Shipley (III).

items.title: Mock #20 · Q5
items.stem:
Arrange the following universities in chronological order in terms of offering courses on Indian English Writing.
A. Central Institute of English, Hyderabad
B. University of Mysore
C. Karnataka University
D. Andhra University
E. Osmania University
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The commonly cited sequence is Andhra University first, then Mysore, the Central Institute of English (CIEFL), Karnataka University and Osmania University. This sequence is taken from a published answer (Testbook).

items.title: Mock #20 · Q6
items.stem:
Thomas Babington Macaulay, the writer of the infamous Minute of 1835, finds a mention
in Salman Rushdie's
items.explanation: In Salman Rushdie's The Moor's Last Sigh (1995), the Anglophile character Aires Mascarenhas reflects on Thomas Babington Macaulay's 1835 Minute on Indian Education, playing on the transformation of 'Macaulay's Minutemen' into 'Macauley's tin-men' in post-independence India.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q7
items.meta: Unit V: Language: Basic Concepts, Theories and Pedagogy
items.stem: Which of the following is not correct about “Cognitive approach to language learning” ?
options: It lays emphasis on conscious acquisition of language
It seeks intellectual understanding by the learner
It rejects the teaching of grammar and language rules
It seeks a reasonable understanding of structure of the language to develop better use of language
items.explanation: The cognitive approach to language acquisition emphasizes conscious mental understanding and internalizing structural rules and grammar. Saying that it rejects the teaching of grammar and language rules is false, as explicit understanding of language structure is central to the cognitive model.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q8
items.stem: "A man can be destroyed but not defeated". Which of the following texts glorifies this as its predominant theme?
options: The Old Man and the Sea
items.explanation: In Ernest Hemingway's novella The Old Man and the Sea (1952), aging Cuban fisherman Santiago declares during his epic struggle with the giant marlin and sharks: 'But man is not made for defeat. A man can be destroyed but not defeated.'

items.title: Mock #20 · Q9
items.stem:
Who, among these, are songwriters who have been awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature?
A. Elton John
B. Rabindranath Tagore
C. Bob Dylan
D. Bob Marley

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Bengali polymath Rabindranath Tagore (who composed over two thousand Rabindra Sangeet songs and won the 1913 Nobel Prize, B) and American singer-songwriter Bob Dylan (awarded the 2016 Nobel Prize, C) are both Nobel Literature laureates.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q10
items.stem: Which of the following poems by Tennyson does NOT speak of old age and death ?
items.explanation: Alfred, Lord Tennyson's short two-stanza ballad 'The Beggar Maid' (1842) simply recounts King Cophetua stepping down from his throne to wed a barefoot beggar girl. In contrast, 'The Lotos-Eaters,' 'Ulysses,' and 'Tithonus' all profoundly meditate on aging, weariness, and mortality.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q11
items.meta: Unit IX: Literary Theory post World War II
items.stem:
Match the following :
Terms
Description
(a)
Ambiguity
(i)
A term coined by Julia Kristeva to refer to the fact
that texts are constituted by a “tissue of citations”.
(b)
Aporia
(ii)
A term used by Mikhail Bakhtin to describe the
variety of languages and voices within a novel.
(c)
Intertextuality
(iii)
An irresolvable internal contradiction or logical
disjunction in a text, usually associated with
deconstructive thinking.
(d)
eteroglossia
(iv)
A term made famous by William Empson to
indicate that a word, phrase, or text can be
interpreted in more than one way.
(a)
(b)
(c)
(d)
items.explanation: Ambiguity was defined by William Empson in Seven Types of Ambiguity (iv); Aporia is deconstruction's term for an irresolvable textual contradiction (iii); Intertextuality was coined by Julia Kristeva (i); and Heteroglossia was formulated by Mikhail Bakhtin (ii).

items.title: Mock #20 · Q12
items.stem:
The Latin epic Aeneid by Virgil?
A. incorporates various legends of Aeneas and makes him the founder of Roman greatness
B. Relates the story of the legendary founding of Rome.
C. relates the story of the legendary founding of Lavinium.
D. recounts the story of Aeneas’ journey in the first 6 books of the epic, and these 6 books are patterned after Homer’s Odyssey
E. recounts the story of Aeneas’ journey in the last 6 books of the epic, and these 6 books are patterned after Homer’s Odyssey
items.explanation: Virgil's Aeneid links Trojan legend to the destiny of Rome, establishing Aeneas as the ancestor of Roman greatness (A) and recounting his founding of Lavinium (C), whereas Rome itself was founded later by Romulus. Additionally, the first six books recount Aeneas's wanderings modeled on Homer's Odyssey (D), while the last six recount warfare modeled on the Iliad.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q13
items.stem:
Who among the following are referred to as the “Scottish Chaucerians” ?
(i) Thomas Hoccleve
(ii) Robert Henryson
(iii) John Lydgate
(iv) William Dunbar
The right combination according to the code is :
items.explanation: Robert Henryson and William Dunbar were Scottish poets who followed Chaucer. Hoccleve and Lydgate were English Chaucerians.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q14
items.stem: Which of the following themes was not common to the works of Cavalier poets such as Thomas Carew, Sir John Denham, Edmund Waller, Sir John Suckling, James Shirley, Richard Lovelace, and Robert Herrick ?
options: Courtly ideals of the good life
items.explanation: Cavalier poetry is about courtly life, carpe diem and royalist loyalty. Pious devotion is typical of the Metaphysical religious poets instead.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q15
items.stem:
Arrange the following works of Dr. B.R. Ambedkar in the correct chronological order of their publication.
A. Mr. Gandhi and Emancipation of Untouchables
B. The Annihilation of Caste
C. The Problem of the Rupee: Its Origin and its Solution
D. Federation Versus Freedom
E. Buddha and his Dhamma
Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: The chronological order of Dr. B. R. Ambedkar's works is: The Problem of the Rupee (C, 1923), Annihilation of Caste (B, 1936), Federation Versus Freedom (D, 1939), Mr. Gandhi and the Emancipation of the Untouchables (A, 1943), and The Buddha and His Dhamma (E, 1957), giving C, B, D, A, E.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q16
items.stem: The Norman Conquest was a significant landmark in English history. What French did the Normans speak and what was it known as?
options: They spoke standard French (of mainland France). Their French was very sweet and musical.
They spoke Norman French (Anglo-Norman). Theirs was certainly not the standard French.
They spoke normal French, rather distinct from Anglo-Norman, another standard language.
They spoke a dialectal French (also called Anglo-Frisian), somewhat closer to the Parisian.
items.explanation: The Normans spoke a northern French dialect, Norman French, which developed into Anglo-Norman in England.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q17
items.stem: The line – “He who works for sweetness and light united, works to make reason and the will of God prevail”, occurs in :
options: Julia Kristeva’s Revolution in Poetic Language
Sigmund Freud’s Civilization and Its Discontents
items.explanation: This statement appears in Chapter 1 ("Sweetness and Light") of Matthew Arnold's Culture and Anarchy (1869), where Arnold borrows Jonathan Swift's phrase to define true culture as the harmonious pursuit of beauty (sweetness) and intellectual clarity (light) to make reason prevail.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q18
items.stem: Who among the following Dickens characters appears as a ghost?
items.explanation: In Charles Dickens's novella A Christmas Carol (1843), Ebenezer Scrooge is first visited on Christmas Eve by the chained ghost of his deceased business partner, Jacob Marley.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q19
items.stem:
Which two of the following poems are by Robert Browning?
A. "Locksley Hall"

B. "The Pied Piper of Hamelin®

C. "The Lady of Shalott"

D. "Two in the Campagna"

Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: 'The Pied Piper of Hamelin' (published in Dramatic Lyrics, 1842) and 'Two in the Campagna' (published in Men and Women, 1855) are poems by Robert Browning. By contrast, 'Locksley Hall' (1842) and 'The Lady of Shalott' (1832/1842) were written by his Victorian contemporary Alfred, Lord Tennyson.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q20
items.stem:
Which two writers can be described as writing historical novels ?

I.
Sir Walter Scott
II.
Charlotte Bronte

III.
Maria Edgeworth
IV. Jane Austen

The right combination according to the code is
items.explanation: Sir Walter Scott (I) established the European historical novel with Waverley (1814) and its successors, and he explicitly acknowledged in his postscript to Waverley that he was inspired to do for Scotland what Anglo-Irish novelist Maria Edgeworth (III) had done for Ireland's history and society in Castle Rackrent (1800).

items.title: Mock #20 · Q21
items.stem:
Match List I with List II

List 1 |List 1

A."Monuments of unaging intellect" I. "Leda and the Swan"

B. "In the foul rag-and-bone shop of the heart" |II. "Adam's Curse"

IC. "So mastered by the brute blood of the air" lin. "Sailing to Byzantium"

ID. "As weary-hearted as that hollow moon" _|IV. "The Circus Animals' Desertion"
Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: In W. B. Yeats's poetry, 'Monuments of unageing intellect' appears in 'Sailing to Byzantium' (1928, A-III), and 'In the foul rag-and-bone shop of the heart' concludes 'The Circus Animals' Desertion' (1939, B-IV). 'So mastered by the brute blood of the air' is from 'Leda and the Swan' (1924, C-I), and 'As weary-hearted as that hollow moon' is from 'Adam's Curse' (1902, D-II).

items.title: Mock #20 · Q22
items.stem:
The quintessentially metafictional novel, If On a Winter's Night a Traveller by Italo
Calvino has alternate chapters with chapter numbers and titles. Which of the following are
the titles of the chapters in the novel ?

I.
Looks Down in the Gathering Shadow

II.
In a Network of Lines that Enlace

III.
In a Network of Lines that Interface

IV.
What Story there Awaits its End ?

The right combination according to the code is
items.explanation: In Italo Calvino's metafictional novel If on a winter's night a traveler (1979), the ten embedded novel fragments include 'Looks down in the gathering shadow' (I) and 'In a network of lines that enlace' (II). The other two actual titles in William Weaver's translation are 'In a network of lines that intersect' and 'What story down there awaits its end?'

items.title: Mock #20 · Q23
items.stem:
What statement(s) are true about liberal humanism?

A. Language is not constitutive

B. There is no fixed and absolute truth. No unalterable essences at all

C. Our mind is an empty state and all enquiry into the artistic phenomenon is objective.

D. Itis language that shapes the reality and not the other way round

E. Truth is not provisional

Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below
items.explanation: In liberal humanism (as summarized by Peter Barry in Beginning Theory), human nature and truth are viewed as timeless and unchanging essences rather than provisional (E), and the critical mind is regarded as an autonomous, objective observer capable of disinterested evaluation (C). Statements B and D reflect post-structuralist critiques that directly oppose liberal humanism.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q24
items.stem: Who among the following coined the term 'Stream of Consciousness'?
items.explanation: While philosopher William James coined the phrase in Principles of Psychology (1890), novelist and critic May Sinclair was the first to apply 'stream of consciousness' to literature in her April 1918 review of Dorothy Richardson's Pointed Roofs in The Egoist.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q25
items.stem:
Arrange the following literary texts in the order of their publication :
(A) The Dunciad
(B) Essay on Man
(C) The Rape of the Lock
(D) Epistle to Dr. Arbuthnot
(E) Windsor Forest
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Pope published The Rape of the Lock (1712), Windsor Forest (1713), The Dunciad (1728), Essay on Man (1733) and Epistle to Dr. Arbuthnot (1735). So C, E, A, B, D.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q26
items.stem: Brij V. Lal's Rama's Banishment deals with the history of Fiji of a time period of _______.
items.explanation: Indo-Fijian historian Brij V. Lal edited Rama's Banishment: A Centenary Tribute to the Fiji Indians, 1879–1979 (1979) on the centenary of Girmitiya indenture in Fiji, though the official NTA answer key marked Option 3 (150 years).

items.title: Mock #20 · Q27
items.stem:
Assertion (A) :
Arts will often work obliquely, by myth or symbol. They may make their
best ‘criticism of life’ simply by being; they may best state by not stating.
Reason (R) :
It follows, if even only part of all this is true, that the arts do have an
important social function. [...] Arts can ive reater depth to a society’s
sense of itself. [...] A country without great art might be a powerful collection
of thriving earthworms but would be a sorry society.
options: Reason (R) is perfectly aligned with Assertion (A)
items.explanation: In cultural and aesthetic theory (echoing Richard Hoggart and Matthew Arnold), Assertion (A) argues that arts criticize life obliquely through imaginative form, and Reason (R) directly explains why this oblique aesthetic operation fulfills a vital, indispensable social function.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q28
items.stem:
The letter 'A' in The Scarlet Letter
stands for
I.
Adultery
II.
Able
III.
Angel
IV.
Appetite
The correct combination for the
statement, according to the code, is
options: I, II and III are correct
I, II and IV are correct
items.explanation: In Nathaniel Hawthorne's The Scarlet Letter (1850), Hester Prynne's scarlet 'A' originally stands for 'Adultery' (I), is later reinterpreted by the townspeople as 'Able' (II) for her selfless charity, and is seen in the sky as 'Angel' (III) at Governor Winthrop's death.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q29
items.stem:
Which two of the following conform to liberal humanist thought?
A. Literature transcends the limits of the age of its origin and so is timeless.
B. Literature is untouched by the essential human nature which is unchanging.
C. Literature is devoid of any purpose to enhance life or promote human values.
D. Identity is a unique essence unaffected by environment and society.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: As outlined in Peter Barry's Beginning Theory, liberal humanism holds that great literature is timeless and transcends its historical moment (A) and that human identity is a fixed, unique essence prior to social and environmental forces (D).

items.title: Mock #20 · Q30
items.stem: Which of the following had the alternative title Things as They Are?
options: Horace Walpole’s The Castle of Otranto
items.explanation: William Godwin's Caleb Williams (1794) is subtitled 'Things as They Are'.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q31
items.stem:
Match the column:
A. Thick description
B. Transcendental signified
C. Vehicle, Tenor
D. Alienation Effect
I. Jacques Derrida
II. A Richards
III. Bertolt Brecht
IV. Clifford Geertz
items.explanation: These critical and theoretical concepts match their originators: Clifford Geertz introduced 'thick description' in cultural anthropology (A-IV, 1973), Jacques Derrida coined the 'transcendental signified' in deconstruction (B-I, 1967), I. A. Richards defined 'tenor and vehicle' in metaphor theory (C-II, 1936), and Bertolt Brecht developed the 'alienation effect' (*Verfremdungseffekt*) for epic theatre (D-III).

items.title: Mock #20 · Q32
items.stem: The character who discusses the relative merits of French drama and English drama in Essay of Dramatic Poesy is:
items.explanation: In John Dryden's Of Dramatick Poesie, An Essay (1668), the debate comparing the relative merits of French and English drama is conducted between Lisideius (representing Sir Charles Sedley, who praises French neoclassical drama) and Neander (Dryden, who defends English drama and tragicomedy).

items.title: Mock #20 · Q33
items.stem:
Black Feminism pays attention to :
(A) The material lives of Black women
(B) The patriarchal nature of black society and traditions
(C) The growth of individualism
(D) The possibilities of 'Sisterhood' of black women
(E) Conforming to hetero sexual relationship only
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Black Feminism focuses on the material realities of Black women's lives (A), critiques patriarchal structures within Black communities and traditions (B), and fosters the solidarity or 'Sisterhood' of Black women (D), corresponding to (A), (B) and (D) Only.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q34
items.stem:
Samuel Johnson has the following to say about an English poet :
"These images are marked by glittering accumulations of ungraceful ornaments : they strike,
rather than please.  The images are magnified by affectation : the language is laboured into
harshness.  The mind of the writer seems to work  with unnatural violence - 'Double, double,
toil and trouble'.  He has a kind of strutting dignity, and is tall by walking on tiptoe.  His art
and his struggle are too visible, and there is too little appearance of ease and nature."
Identify the poet
items.explanation: In his 'Life of Gray' from Lives of the Most Eminent English Poets (1781), Samuel Johnson harshly criticized Thomas Gray's Pindaric odes ('The Progress of Poesy' and 'The Bard') for artificial diction and strained sublimity, remarking that Gray 'has a kind of strutting dignity, and is tall by walking on tiptoe'.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q35
items.stem:
Arrange the following in the chronological order of publication:
A. Aspects of the Theory of Syntax

B. Course in General Linguistics

C.Semiotics and the Philosophy of Language

D. How to Do Things with Words

Choose the correct answer from the options given below
items.explanation: Ferdinand de Saussure's Course in General Linguistics (B) was published posthumously in 1916, followed by J. L. Austin's speech-act lectures How to Do Things with Words (D) in 1962. Noam Chomsky's Aspects of the Theory of Syntax (A) appeared in 1965, and Umberto Eco's Semiotics and the Philosophy of Language (C) was published in 1984.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q36
items.stem: How many major forms of drama have been described by Bharata in his manual of dramaturgy?
items.explanation: In Chapter 18 of the Natyashastra, Bharata Muni classifies classical Indian drama into ten major dramatic forms (Dasa Rupaka): Nataka, Prakarana, Bhana, Prahasana, Dima, Vyayoga, Samavakara, Vithi, Anka, and Ihamriga.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q37
items.stem:
Assertion (A) : At the end of Heart of Darkness, Marlow tells a lie to the Intended about Kurtz when he tells her "The last word he pronounced was – your name".
Reason (R) : Marlow tells this lie because he is secretly in love with the Intended and tells her what she wants to hear.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true ; (R) is the correct explanation.
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation.
items.explanation: At the close of Joseph Conrad's Heart of Darkness (1899), Marlow indeed lies to Kurtz's Intended by telling her that Kurtz's final word was her name rather than 'The horror! The horror!' in order to preserve her saving illusion (the Official UGC Key marks Option B, though textually Marlow acts out of pity rather than romantic love).

items.title: Mock #20 · Q38
items.stem: Edward Brathwaite’s poem “Calypso” assumes that you are familiar with __________.
options: the business of Calypso during the Middle Passage
the folk ways and mores of Trinidadian merchants
the West Indian music in syncopated African rhythm
items.explanation: Barbadian poet Kamau Brathwaite's poem 'Calypso' (from The Arrivants) uses syncopated polyrhythms, steel-pan cadences, and Creole speech patterns rooted in the Afro-Caribbean musical tradition of Trinidadian calypso.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q39
items.stem:
Which of the following statements are correctly matched with the texts:
A. "(T)he poet is the food for the tenderest stomachs; the poet is indeed the right popular philosopher" – "An Apology for Poetry".
B. "This essay proposes to halt at the frontier of metaphysics or mysticism, and confine itself to such practical conclusions as can be applied by the responsible person interested in poetry." – "The Metaphysical Poets"
C. "The invaluable works of our elder writers, I had almost said the works of Shakespeare and Milton, are driven into neglect by frantic novels, sickly and stupid German Tragedies, and deluges of idle and extravagant stories in verse." – "Preface to Lyrical Ballads"
D. For "poetry the idea is everything; the rest is a world of illusion, of divine illusion. Poetry attaches its emotion to the idea; the idea is the fact." – "The Study of Poetry"
E. "A fool might once himself alone expose / Now one in verse makes many more in prose." – "Essay on Man"
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: Quotes A, C, and D are correctly matched to Sidney's An Apology for Poetry, Wordsworth's Preface to Lyrical Ballads, and Arnold's 'The Study of Poetry'. Quote B is from T. S. Eliot's 'Tradition and the Individual Talent' and Quote E is from Alexander Pope's An Essay on Criticism.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q40
items.stem: The debate on 'the condition of England question' was initiated by
items.explanation: Victorian sage writer Thomas Carlyle coined the phrase and initiated the debate on the 'Condition-of-England Question' in the opening chapter of his 1839 pamphlet Chartism, addressing the social misery of the industrial working class.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q41
items.stem:
Match the column:
(Texts)
A. Bodies that Matter
B. A World of Difference
C. A Literature of their Own
D. Vamps and Tramps
(Author)
I. Barbara Johnson
II. Judith Butler
III. Camille Paglia
IV. Elaine Showalter
items.explanation: Judith Butler wrote Bodies That Matter: On the Discursive Limits of "Sex" (1993) (A-II); Barbara Johnson wrote A World of Difference (1987) (B-I); Elaine Showalter published A Literature of Their Own (1977) (C-IV); and Camille Paglia authored Vamps & Tramps (1994) (D-III). This gives A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q42
items.stem: Who said that “Shakespeare was the Homer, or father of our dramatic poets; Johnson was the Vergil, the pattern of elaborate writing”?
items.explanation: John Dryden made this celebrated comparative assessment through the character of Neander in *An Essay of Dramatic Poesy* (1668), praising Shakespeare's organic, comprehensive imagination as akin to Homer's, while likening Ben Jonson's learned classical discipline to Virgil's.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q43
items.meta: Unit IX: Literary Theory post World War II
items.stem:
(a)
Jean Baudrillard tells us that postmodern societies are marked by simulacra.
(b)
By simulacra he means non-representations of reality.
(c)
Simulacra artificially produce a mediated world masquerading as authenticity.
(d)
It was not Jean Baudrillard but his interpreters who coined the term “simulacra”.
Which of the above statements are true ?
items.explanation: In Simulacra and Simulation (1981), French cultural theorist Jean Baudrillard argues that postmodernity is marked by simulacra (a), which artificially manufacture a hyperreal world that masks the total absence of profound reality (c); statements (a) and (c) are true.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q44
items.stem: What is meant by "Corporate author" in research?
options: A writer who belongs to a corporate company
A writer who writes on matters of corporate affairs
A work produced by an institution, an association or a government agency
items.explanation: In research methodology and bibliographic citation (such as MLA style), a 'corporate author' refers to an institution, commission, association, corporation, or government agency that produces a work in its collective name without attributing it to an individual personal author.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q45
items.stem:
Identify the correct chronological order as per the publication years of the following works:
A. Characteristics of Men, Manners, Opinions and Times
B. The Advancement of Learning
C. Inquiry into the Original of our Idea of Beauty and Virtues
D. The Plan of a Dictionary of the English Language
items.explanation: The chronological sequence of these philosophical and literary works by publication year is: Francis Bacon's *The Advancement of Learning* (B, 1605), Lord Shaftesbury's *Characteristics of Men, Manners, Opinions and Times* (A, 1711), Francis Hutcheson's *Inquiry into the Original of our Idea of Beauty and Virtues* (C, 1725), and Samuel Johnson's *The Plan of a Dictionary of the English Language* (D, 1747).

items.title: Mock #20 · Q46
items.stem: Who has described his criticism as a “by-product” of his “private poetry-workshop” and as “a prolongation of the thinking that went into the formation of my own verse”?
items.explanation: T. S. Eliot described his critical writing in his 1956 lecture 'The Frontiers of Criticism' (published in *On Poetry and Poets*, 1957) as a 'by-product' of his 'private poetry-workshop', explaining that his literary essays were extensions of the practical problems he encountered in writing verse.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q47
items.stem:
Given below are two statements:
Statement I: The Indian English novelists witnessed a warm reception of their writings in Europe, and they proliferated well in India during the 1930's and 1940's.
Statement II: The two world wars added an overall sense of gloom and civilisational crisis across the globe, especially in Europe.

In light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
items.explanation: The 1930s and 1940s saw the flourishing of the first major generation of Indian English novelists—Mulk Raj Anand, R. K. Narayan, and Raja Rao—whose works were published and praised in Britain and Europe (Statement I is true), while the two World Wars simultaneously generated a pervasive sense of civilizational crisis across Europe (Statement II is true).

items.title: Mock #20 · Q48
items.stem:
Who wrote the following about Rousseau?
"Like his favorite philosopher, Plato, Rousseau sought to discover and produce the moral man who would make the moral society, and a moral society that would foster the moral man."
items.explanation: Enlightenment historian Peter Gay wrote this assessment of Jean-Jacques Rousseau in The Enlightenment: An Interpretation (1969), comparing Rousseau's dual project in Emile and The Social Contract to Plato's Republic.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q49
items.stem:

B. The director
C. Fan clubs

items.explanation: In Pierre Bourdieu's sociology of culture, film magazine columnists (A) and organized fan clubs (C) act as 'cultural intermediaries' who mediate reception and shape taste between primary film producers (the director and producer) and the public.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q50
items.stem:
From which poem are the following lines extracted?

“Some are bewildered in the maze of schools,
And some made coxcombs Nature meant but fools,
In search of wit these lose their common sense
And then turn critics in their own defense”
items.explanation: These heroic couplets appear in Part I (lines 26–29) of Alexander Pope's masterwork An Essay on Criticism (1711), where he cautions against superficial learning and pseudo-critics who turn to criticism out of disappointed wit.

items.explanation: Escape from Earth and The English Ghost are non-fiction. The Great Fire of London and English Music are novels.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q54
items.stem: Who wrote the famous text Dignity of Man ?
items.explanation: Thomas More translated Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's Life of John Picus Earl of Mirandula into English around 1505, introducing Renaissance humanist ideas regarding human dignity into English literature. More's humanist writings, including Utopia, consistently defend human dignity and reason.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q55

B. Intermittent closure
C. Complete closure and sudden release
D. Complete closure and slow release
E. Open Approximation
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
items.explanation: The usual textbook order is plosive (complete closure, sudden release), affricate (complete closure, slow release), fricative (close approximation), approximant (open approximation) and then roll or trill (intermittent closure).

items.title: Mock #20 · Q56

options: It is the sick man of Indian English literature
It is deeply rooted in the Indian folk tradition
It is essentially a diasporic phenomenon
items.explanation: In Indian English Literature: 1980-2000: A Critical Survey (2001), critics M. K. Naik and Shyamala A. Narayan famously characterize Indian English drama as 'the sick man of Indian English literature' due to the enduring dearth of performable original stage plays.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q57
items.stem:
Given below are two statements. One is labeled as Assertion A and the other is labeled as Reason R.
Assertion (A): The experience of homosexuality in a homophobic culture is not the same for the whites and blacks.
Reason (R): Sexuality and sexual identity is experienced differently by the whites and blacks.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the option given below:
options: Both (A) and (R) are correct and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are correct but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
(A) is correct but (R) is not correct.
(A) is not correct but (R) is correct.
items.explanation: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A): as intersectional queer theory demonstrates, racial identity shapes how sexuality and sexual identity are lived and perceived, meaning that Black and white LGBTQ+ individuals experience homophobia differently.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q58
items.stem: Which among the following texts is not based on the theme of disability?
options: Gabrielle Zevin's Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow
Julia Heaberlin's We are All the Same in the Dark
items.explanation: George Bernard Shaw's play Mrs. Warren's Profession (1893) focuses on the economic factors driving prostitution and women's limited employment choices rather than disability. In contrast, Madeleine Ryan's A Room Called Earth (autism), Gabrielle Zevin's Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow (chronic physical pain and disability), and Julia Heaberlin's We Are All the Same in the Dark (limb amputation) all center on physical or neurodivergent disability.

Statement (a) is incorrect because Buddenbrooks is set across the 19th century (1835–1877).

items.title: Mock #20 · Q73

items.explanation: The historical sequence of these classical Sanskrit poetics treatises is: Bharata's Natyashastra (c. 2nd century BCE-2nd century CE), Bhamaha's Kavyalankara (c. 7th century CE), Anandavardhana's Dhvanyaloka (9th century CE), Kuntaka's Vakroktijivitam (late 10th-early 11th century CE), and Kshemendra's Aucityavicharacharcha (11th century CE) [(A), (C), (E), (D), (B)].

Break any of these rules sooner than say anything outright barbarous
If it is possible to cut a word out, always cut it out
items.explanation: Near the conclusion of his 1946 essay 'Politics and the English Language', George Orwell sets out six practical rules for clear writing, ending with the famous sixth rule: '(vi) Break any of these rules sooner than say anything outright barbarous.'

items.title: Mock #20 · Q91
items.stem:
[Read the following lines from William Wordsworth's "Lines Composed a Few Miles above Tintern Abbey" (1798) carefully and answer the question that follows:]

"For I have learned
To look on nature, not as in the hour
Of thoughtless youth; but hearing oftentimes
The still, sad music of humanity,
Nor harsh nor grating, though of ample power
To chasten and subdue. And I have felt
A presence that disturbs me with the joy
Of elevated thoughts; a sense sublime
Of something far more deeply interfused,
Whose dwelling is the light of setting suns,
And the round ocean and the living air,
And the blue sky, and in the mind of man:
A motion and a spirit, that impels
All thinking things, all objects of all thought,
And rolls through all things."

In this passage, what fundamental transition in the poet's relationship with nature is described?
options: A shift from sensory delight in wild nature to a moral and spiritual awareness infused with human sympathy
A total disillusionment with natural landscapes in favour of industrial urban life
A rejection of pantheism in favour of strict orthodox theological dogma
An emotional breakdown caused by childhood grief
items.explanation: Wordsworth contrasts the 'thoughtless youth' of purely physical/sensory passion with mature contemplation, where nature becomes imbued with 'the still, sad music of humanity' and a sublime spiritual presence.

The collaborative agency of human imagination interacting with external reality to construct experience
The superiority of scientific instruments over human senses
items.explanation: Wordsworth asserts the creative epistemology of Romanticism: perception is not merely passive reflection, but an active, collaborative interplay between external sensory objects and the creative power of the human mind.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q96
items.meta: Unit IV / Unit VIII: Prose & Criticism
items.stem:
[Read the following passage from Matthew Arnold's "The Study of Poetry" (1880) carefully and answer the question that follows:]

"The future of poetry is immense, because in poetry, where it is worthy of its high destinies, our race, as time goes on, will find an ever surer and surer stay. There is not a creed which is not shaken, not an accredited dogma which is not shown to be questionable, not a received tradition which does not threaten to dissolve. Our religion has materialised itself in the fact, in the supposed fact; it has attached its emotion to the fact, and now the fact is failing it. But for poetry the idea is everything; the rest is a world of illusion, of divine illusion. Poetry attaches its emotion to the idea; the idea is the fact. The strongest part of our religion to-day is its unconscious poetry... More and more mankind will discover that we have to turn to poetry to interpret life for us, to console us, to sustain us."

According to Matthew Arnold in this passage, why is "the future of poetry immense"?
options: Because poetry will become the primary commercial product of the industrial economy
Because verse drama will replace newspapers as the chief source of information
Because science will definitively prove all theological dogmas through poetry
Because as religious dogmas and traditional creeds collapse, mankind will rely on high poetry to interpret, console, and sustain life
items.explanation: Arnold argues that as accredited religious dogmas and creeds are shaken, humanity will increasingly depend on poetry's spiritual power to interpret life, console grief, and sustain faith.

[Arnold's "The Study of Poetry"]
What famous definition of poetry does Matthew Arnold propound in this landmark critical essay?
options: A speaking picture with this end, to teach and delight
A criticism of life under the conditions fixed for such a criticism by the laws of poetic truth and poetic beauty
The spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings recollected in tranquillity
A structure of complex verbal ambiguities and paradoxes
items.explanation: Arnold famously defines poetry as 'a criticism of life under the conditions fixed for such a criticism by the laws of poetic truth and poetic beauty.'

items.title: Mock #20 · Q98
items.meta: Unit IV / Unit VIII: Prose & Criticism
items.stem:
[Arnold's "The Study of Poetry"]
To detect the highest excellence in poetry and guard against false estimates, Arnold introduces which famous comparative critical method?
items.explanation: Arnold introduces the 'Touchstone Method'—keeping short passages and lines from supreme masters (Homer, Dante, Shakespeare, Milton) in mind to test the genuine poetic quality of other poets.

items.title: Mock #20 · Q99

items.stem:
[Arnold's "The Study of Poetry"]
Which major English poet does Arnold praise for possessing supreme 'virtue of manner and movement' and divine fluidity, yet fault for lacking 'high seriousness' (spoudaiotes)?
items.explanation: Arnold praises Chaucer's large, free, simple, clear view of human life, but explicitly denies him a place among the supreme classics because Chaucer's poetry 'lacks the high seriousness' found in Dante and Shakespeare.

[Arnold's "The Study of Poetry"]
Which two misleading estimates does Arnold warn critics against when seeking the real estimate of a poem's worth?
options: The Historical estimate and the Personal estimate
The Structural estimate and the Deconstructive estimate
The Aesthetic estimate and the Moral estimate
The Formalist estimate and the Marxist estimate
items.explanation: Arnold warns that critics frequently fall into two fallacies: the 'historical estimate' (overvaluing a work due to its historical developmental significance) and the 'personal estimate' (overvaluing a work due to personal affinities or prejudices).
